name: PCR Annealing Temperature Calculator
seoTitle: PCR Annealing Temperature Calculator — Formula & Results
seoDesc: Annealing temperature is the one PCR variable worth calculating: too low and you get primer dimers and non-specific bands, too high and you get nothing. Free
summary:
Annealing temperature is the one PCR variable worth calculating: too low and you get primer dimers and non-specific bands, too high and you get nothing. It returns annealing temperature, gradient low, gradient high and tm difference, and the panel shows all of them at once.

This calculator uses the primer pair's melting temperatures, the salt and the product length to suggest a starting temperature and a gradient to test. Every result is derived from the boxes you fill in, so changing one input updates the whole panel at once. Units are stated on every box and in every result, so a figure copied out of a protocol, a datasheet or a chart can be entered without converting it first.

sections.title: The formula behind the PCR Annealing Temperature
sections.html:
Ta = min(Tm) − 5 °C; test a gradient of Ta ± 3 °C

The symbols in the formula
SymbolWhat it stands forUnit
Tmmelting temperature of each primer°C
offsethow far below Tm to anneal°C
Taannealing temperature°C

sections.title: How do I use the PCR Annealing Temperature?
sections.html:
The form asks only for what the formula needs — nothing is optional decoration.

  1. Enter the values you already have. Every box accepts a decimal point and a minus sign; thousands separators are ignored.
  2. The grey boxes are results: they are worked out from your inputs and cannot be typed into.
  3. Press Calculate. The results fill in together, and from then on they follow every edit you make — there is no page to reload and nothing to submit.

sections.title: A worked example
sections.html:
Take the default values the page opens with: forward primer tm of 60°C, reverse primer tm of 60°C, offset below the lower tm of 5°C, product length of 400 bp.

Substituting them into the formula gives annealing temperature of 55°C, gradient low of 52°C, gradient high of 58°C, tm difference of 0°C, extension time (taq, 1 min per kb) of 24 s, cycling time for 30 cycles of 12 min.

The arithmetic is the page's own: change one box and the result moves by the amount the formula implies, which is the quickest way to convince yourself the tool is honest.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
A raw figure only means something next to the bands it is normally judged against. Here is the scale that goes with this one:

How to read the result
ResultBandWhat it means
Tm gap under 2 °CGood pairboth primers anneal at the same temperature
2 – 5 °CAcceptableuse the lower Tm and expect reduced efficiency
above 5 °CPoor pairredesign; a long product will not amplify efficiently

  • Use the lower of the two Tms, and 5 °C below it as a starting point. The first cycles matter more than the rest, so a two-step or touchdown protocol can rescue a difficult pair.

  • Salt matters: Tm rises about 16.6 °C per log unit of monovalent cation concentration, so a primer quoted in 50 mM Na⁺ is not the same in a 1× Q5 buffer.

  • Add 3 °C if the primers are longer than 22 nt or the product is GC-rich; subtract it for AT-rich templates.

  • Two-step PCR (denature, then anneal/extend at 68–72 °C) is becoming standard for high-fidelity polymerases that extend quickly.

sections.title: What are the common mistakes?
sections.html:
The arithmetic is simple; the inputs are where things go wrong. The usual culprits:

  • Averaging the two Tms instead of using the lower one.
  • Using the manufacturer's default 60 °C for every pair — it works often enough to hide the pairs it fails.
  • Changing several variables at once when a single gradient would identify the problem.

faq.q: Should annealing temperature be higher or lower than Tm?
faq.a: Lower, usually 3–5 °C below the lower primer's Tm.

faq.q: Why does my product vanish at higher annealing temperatures?
faq.a: Because the primers no longer bind; the temperature is above their Tm in your buffer.
A program that starts 10 °C above the annealing temperature and steps down, which favours the specific product early and prevents primer dimers later.

faq.q: What does the PCR Annealing Temperature actually calculate?
faq.a: It returns annealing temperature, gradient low, gradient high and tm difference. Each one is derived by the formula on this page, so you can check any figure by hand.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — and if you change an input, every result updates with it.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. This calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.
